question: What is the primary focus of human factors in nursing?

options.A: Increasing the daily number of patient bed turnovers
options.B: Reducing the total hospital budget for medical equipment
options.C: Improving interactions between workers, tools, and environments
options.D: Punishing staff members who make medication administration errors

explanation: Human factors study how people interact with equipment and workspaces to optimize both safety and performance. [learn more](GST319_U5_T7#GST319_U5_T7_h1)

question: Why does human factors engineering focus on the system rather than blaming the individual?

options.A: Hospital management protects nurses from legal liability entirely
options.B: Individual staff members never actually cause adverse events
options.C: Technology replaces the need for clinical judgment in practice
options.D: System designs often set up workers to make predictable mistakes

explanation: Examining systemic flaws helps redesign workflows so that human errors are caught or prevented before harming patients. [learn more](GST319_U5_T7#GST319_U5_T7_h1)

question: What do the holes in the Swiss Cheese Model represent?

options.A: Active failures and latent system conditions
options.B: Gaps in the hospital physical building structure
options.C: Patient compliance issues during ward admission
options.D: Deliberate sabotage by disgruntled hospital staff

explanation: The holes stand for weaknesses in defenses, such as design flaws or momentary lapses in attention. [learn more](GST319_U5_T7#GST319_U5_T7_h2)

question: When does an adverse patient incident happen according to the Swiss Cheese Model?

options.A: When patient numbers exceed the licensed ward capacity
options.B: When holes in all defensive layers align simultaneously
options.C: When a nurse makes a single medication calculation error
options.D: When hospital management ignores a written safety report

explanation: An error slips through all barriers only when every single safety layer fails at the same time. [learn more](GST319_U5_T7#GST319_U5_T7_h2)

question: What is anchoring bias in a clinical setting?

options.A: Relying solely on hospital policies during an emergency
options.B: Forgetting to secure a patient stretcher during transport
options.C: Refusing to delegate tasks to junior nursing students
options.D: Fixating on an initial impression and ignoring new data

explanation: Anchoring occurs when a clinician locks onto an early diagnosis and fails to adjust when new symptoms appear. [learn more](GST319_U5_T7#GST319_U5_T7_h3)

question: A nurse assumes a patient has malaria simply because three malaria cases were admitted yesterday. Which cognitive bias does this demonstrate?
explanation: The availability heuristic happens when recent or memorable events distort our judgment of current probability. [learn more](GST319_U5_T7#GST319_U5_T7_h3)

question: What is the primary goal of physical ergonomics in healthcare?

options.A: Matching workplace design to human physical and anatomical limits
options.B: Ensuring all nursing uniforms meet international aesthetic standards
options.C: Maximizing the number of patients admitted into a single ward
options.D: Decreasing the financial cost of hospital architectural building plans

explanation: Physical ergonomics adapts the physical environment to protect staff from injury and ease task execution. [learn more](GST319_U5_T7#GST319_U5_T7_h4)

question: Poor ward layouts and disorganized supply cupboards primarily lead to which outcome for nurses?

options.A: Reduced reliance on electronic health record systems
options.B: Increased physical fatigue and delayed emergency responses
options.C: Enhanced critical thinking and faster patient recovery rates
options.D: Better interprofessional collaboration among the medical team

explanation: Bad layouts force extra walking and searching, wasting time and draining physical energy during critical moments. [learn more](GST319_U5_T7#GST319_U5_T7_h4)

question: What does the letter 'R' stand for in the SBAR communication tool?
explanation: SBAR stands for Situation, Background, Assessment, and Recommendation, guiding concise clinical reporting. [learn more](GST319_U5_T7#GST319_U5_T7_h5)

question: Why is closed-loop communication important during emergency resuscitations?

options.A: It eliminates the need for written documentation in the patient chart
options.B: It establishes strict hospital hierarchy between doctors and nurses
options.C: It prevents patients from overhearing sensitive medical discussions
options.D: It ensures medication orders are repeated and confirmed before execution

explanation: Repeating an order back verifies that the recipient heard and understood the instruction correctly. [learn more](GST319_U5_T7#GST319_U5_T7_h5)

question: What is vigilance decrement in a clinical context?

options.A: The gradual loss of clinical knowledge after graduation from nursing school
options.B: The sudden refusal of a nurse to work extra hours on night shift
options.C: The drop in ability to monitor continuous displays or patient changes over time
options.D: The reduction in patient vital sign checks ordered by attending physicians

explanation: Extended monitoring leads to mental exhaustion, making it harder to spot subtle clinical deterioration. [learn more](GST319_U5_T7#GST319_U5_T7_h6)

question: How does chronic fatigue directly affect a nurse's cognitive performance?

options.A: It slows reaction times and impairs working memory capacity
options.B: It enhances the ability to multitask during complex resuscitations
options.C: It permanently improves long-term memory for pharmacology
options.D: It eliminates susceptibility to cognitive confirmation biases

explanation: Tired brains process information slower and struggle to retain temporary details needed for safe care. [learn more](GST319_U5_T7#GST319_U5_T7_h6)

question: What is a forcing function in human factors engineering?

options.A: A design feature that makes an incorrect action impossible to do
options.B: A mandatory overtime schedule enforced during staff shortages
options.C: A physical restraint used for confused patients on the ward
options.D: A strict disciplinary policy for nurses who miss shift handover

explanation: Forcing functions block errors by design, such as connectors that only fit compatible tubing. [learn more](GST319_U5_T7#GST319_U5_T7_h7)

question: Why is redundancy used as a safety strategy in medication administration?

options.A: Hospital accreditation boards require duplicate charting on paper
options.B: It speeds up the overall discharge process for stable patients
options.C: Multiple checks catch mistakes that a single person might miss
options.D: It reduces the financial cost of purchasing expensive drugs

explanation: Redundancy adds backup layers of verification so single lapses do not harm the patient. [learn more](GST319_U5_T7#GST319_U5_T7_h7)

question: What is a key characteristic of a 'just culture' in a hospital?

options.A: Punishment is distributed equally among doctors and nurses regardless of fault
options.B: Managers never investigate adverse events to protect staff feelings
options.C: Every clinical mistake results in immediate termination of employment
options.D: Staff feel safe reporting errors and near-misses without fear of unfair punishment

explanation: A just culture balances individual accountability with learning from systemic errors through open reporting. [learn more](GST319_U5_T7#GST319_U5_T7_h8)

question: Why do resource shortages in Nigerian hospitals often lead to dangerous clinical workarounds?

options.A: Management strictly forbids the use of standard safety checklists
options.B: Patients refuse to purchase prescribed medications from hospital pharmacies
options.C: Nurses improvise with available items to deliver care despite missing supplies
options.D: Staff members prefer using broken equipment to save hospital funds

explanation: Lack of proper tools forces staff to improvise workarounds, bypassing built-in safety checks and increasing risk. [learn more](GST319_U5_T7#GST319_U5_T7_h8)
